title: Will It Be Me?
subtitle: Dementia Risk, Genetic Testing, and Planning Ahead for Your Family
author: Laura Whitfield
topic: What it means for you when a parent, sibling or grandparent has dementia (Alzheimer's, frontotemporal dementia or another form). The book covers how to read your family history and what it says about your own risk and your children's, whether and when to take a genetic test and what to arrange first, how to recognize early changes and get a diagnosis taken seriously, and how to build a family plan for care, work, money and the years ahead.
audience: Adults in the United States, roughly 30 to 65, who have watched dementia reach someone in their family. Often it is a parent diagnosed young, a sibling, or several relatives across generations, and the reader now carries the question of whether it will happen to them and to their children. Many are already helping to care for the person who is ill while holding down a job. Some first heard the name of the disease on a scan report and had to look it up. Others lived with years of other diagnoses before anyone said dementia. A second group is the spouse of a person with dementia who is arranging genetic tests for the children and grandchildren. Neither group is made of science readers. They have the disease at home, they have read the stories, and they want the answers a story can't give for their own case.
promise: The reader comes away with four things. First, a clear picture of what a relative's dementia means for their own risk and their children's: which forms are inherited and which are not, the difference between a gene that causes the disease and a gene that only raises the odds, and what each number really says. Second, what they need to decide, with a genetic counselor, whether and when to be tested, and what to put in place before the result and after it. Third, the signs that call for a medical evaluation and the questions that get a diagnosis taken seriously. Fourth, a practical plan for the family: who cares for whom, the help that exists, work, money and legal papers, and their own future. The goal is to turn waiting into a set of decisions. The book explains and helps the reader decide. It does not promise anything. No test, habit or program in these pages can guarantee that a person will not develop dementia, and the book says so.
tone: Warm, honest and steady, like a genetic counselor who is also a friend. It speaks to the reader as 'you' and takes the fear seriously, without feeding it and without false reassurance. Every percentage is explained in plain words the first time it appears, and every medical term is defined. Chapters open with a scene from one of a few recurring families and then move into the science and the practical steps, so that human story and explanation alternate. It is prose to be read, not bullet lists. Where rules, benefits or protections vary by state, insurer or year, it says so and tells the reader where to check. It never tells the reader whether to be tested. It lays out what each choice involves.
